title: The Buddha Taught Nirvana
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach's main teaching is that true freedom from suffering lies not in changing external circumstances, but rather in transforming our own inner experience of it. This involves recognizing how our thoughts and perceptions add layers of suffering to what would otherwise be a natural part of life, and learning to let go of these burdens through mindfulness and meditation. By doing so, we can cultivate a sense of understanding and compassion that allows us to approach challenges like racism and suffering with wisdom and hope, rather than feeling overwhelmed or hopeless.

sentences.text: Good morning to everyone.
Thank you for joining Zen Alive, and thank you all for your really vigorous and attentive participation in the practice period classes.
It's been wonderful to get to know you and have some sense of your working with the dharma and IkuShun's teachings during this practice period.
I tend to talk too long.

I'm going to ask IkuShun if you would please let me know about the time, normally when you're getting close to the time where people stop for question and answer, because I understand this is one of those opportunities at Cedar to have an exchange.
I'm hoping that I'll be a little bit provocative in what I have to offer you today.
We'll see how it lands on you.

We're a good portion of the way through the practice period, and it's a nice time to circle back around to what we've been studying, to see where we are with the teachings we have been looking at through Thich Nhat Hanh's heart of understanding, the heart of being.
The title of this talk is something about what the Buddha taught.
That's drawn off of a title of a book that was quite popular in the 90s when I started practicing, *What the Buddha Taught*, and my addition is "was really nirvana."
The idea for this talk came from an exchange that happened very recently on the AZT, the Americans and Teachers of America, the Association of Zen Teachers of America, Listserv.
Someone raised the question that the Buddha's first noble truth is really a downer for a lot of people.
People these days, particularly with Western psychology, our Western minds, really don't find much hope or resonance or encouragement from the idea that the first noble truth is suffering.

So I wanted to unpack that a little bit and build in something that [unclear: "Des"] has touched on, and build out a little bit the understanding of the first noble truth that's a little bit different.
It's actually that understanding of the first noble truth, suffering, inside out.
First, I'd like you to take a moment to think for yourself.
What's your idea about what the Buddha meant when he said, life is suffering, or there is invariably suffering in a human existence?
What comes up for you, what hits you in the gut, your first impulse about that?
And then drop down a little more deeply into that.
What's your experience of your own suffering?
Who or what is responsible for that suffering?
What could the Buddha have meant by that?
His life from the outside, as Siddhartha, seemed really great.
He had everything he needed.
He was comfortable.
He had medicine, he had shelter, he had fine food, he had a great future ahead of him.
He was married, presumably to a beautiful wife, because anyone of his stature would have been well situated that way.
And he had the good fortune of his first child being a son.
Was it really that he just escaped the compound one time and saw someone old, sick and dying and wondered about how the other 99 percent lived?
Or maybe he already had a feeling.
Maybe he had a feeling that some of us share in some way.
I've often thought about the name Raula, which was his son's name, which means fetter.
We take that sometimes to mean that his son was a burden.
But how?
Maybe he loved him so much that this pull between a way in which he wanted to live, or a question that was important to him, was in conflict with doing what he wanted to do for his son.
So what is this suffering really about?
Who or what is responsible for your suffering?
And what is your agency in addressing it?
As I was preparing this talk, I reflected back on an insight that I had not so many years ago.
Something happened to me when I was 10 or 11, when I basically went without eating on weekends.
One of my old teachers, who was a friend, asked me why I hadn't packed my own lunch for these outings.
The idea was shocking to me.
I hadn't even considered it as a child.
So there's already something karmic in the thinking about how this problem of suffering gets solved, how this problem of meeting human needs gets solved.
I wonder that for you, too.
What is your suffering?
Who or what is responsible?
And what is your agency in addressing it?
Remember that in all the pages that we can read of the teachings of the Buddha passed along in the Pali Canon, he said that he taught one thing and one thing only: suffering and the end of suffering.

The Buddha was a great psychologist, as we know from reading any of his stories, really appropriate to the situation of whatever the people in his sangha, or the people in the communities that he passed through on his alms rounds and travel, needed.
He was always directing what they needed to do to understand their situation better.
His idea was the medicine to address their suffering.
Buddha's suffering is not, I don't think, the usual way I used to think of my suffering, and maybe we do, generally in society.
Buddha's suffering is really our reaction to our circumstances.
It's not the circumstance itself, but our reaction to our circumstances.
That should probably be a little bit provocative for some people to hear in that way.
The word suffering is one of the Western translations of Dukkha.
I'm not a Pali or Sanskrit scholar, so I can't tell you all the different options that this word might have been or how people arrived at suffering.
I think in some ways in English it's a wonderful combination of both the physical or situational and the mental anguish.
There are elements of both of them in there, and I think that's somewhat confusing.

Gil Fransdal, a Theravadan teacher some of you know, who's well respected and who also is trained in Soto Zen and is a deshi, a Dharma heir of my teacher, says that probably a more accurate word, and he's not alone in that, is the dissatisfaction or discontentment of life.
That probably says it better than suffering.
It may be more accurate to the spiritual discontent or unhappiness that leads one to seek larger answers than their own life, and has brought some of you to join into this meeting today.
I'm reminded of a story that a Zen teacher told when I met her in Tassajara over 20 years ago.
She was a successful dancer with a dance career, but there was something just uneasy to her about her way of life.
She walked into a Hallmark store to find a [unclear: "car"] to purchase, to send, and she was just overwhelmed by all the schlock.
She was overwhelmed by all the silly, not false, but easy sentiment.
And she said, I have to change my life.
Kind of like that.
Sometimes we want relief from our own foibles, our own foible-ridden, self-created unhappiness, and meditation really does provide relief.
Mindfulness really does bring us into the beauty of this perfect moment.
For some people finding that grounding is enough.
Some might call that the healing aspect of practice: to see the sources of suffering that arise in our mind by deeply looking, by deeply coming in to just this present moment.
That allows us to continue on in our life.
Other people have something really different.
I just want to tip my hat to that.

We're all here because we have a special, and I don't mean special like better than other people, I mean our own unique, not rare, orientation towards meeting and understanding how our life fits in the greater workings of things.
I do end of life work, and have been a physician for 40 years, and have had many of these conversations.
I think for many people that greater meaning comes from other kinds of things, perhaps like family.
Sometimes it comes from things that we might consider more trivial.
And that's okay, but that's really not what we're talking about in this talk.
A normal life, we all know, has great difficulties: loss, illness, liability, accidents, misfortunes, misunderstandings and other hardships.
A human life also has contentment, happiness, love, real connection, joy, good luck or just [unclear: "race"].
Human life is not all suffering, and the Buddha was not dumb about that.
Some of it may be related to something we've done directly, or to our habits, or to something impersonal and random, like an earthquake or an accident.
The Buddha's admonition of the first noble truth was related to this ordinary life, but not exactly this, not precisely.
I think probably most of you already have some understanding of this.
Sorrow and grief, and even [unclear: "to spirit times"], come with a package of how humans are made.
There's a famous story of a Rinzai master sometime in the 17th or 18th century, really well regarded, with many, many students.
His young son died suddenly, and he wailed in grief at his son's death.
Many of his students said, my goodness, who is this man?
We thought he was some kind of teacher with some kind of understanding of the coolness of life and the ineffable-ness of it.
And he said, I wouldn't be a human being if I didn't feel for the death of my son.
So this practice is not about losing our emotional connection with any of our life experiences.
There's something extra that is suffering, something extra that we add to life's events.
So ask yourself again, you've been studying the nutriments that Thich Nhat Hanh talks about that feed our suffering mind.
What do you think the nature of suffering really is?
The Buddha famously taught about the first and the second arrows.
I know [unclear: "Nomen Tin"] talks about that a lot, and probably other teachers at Red Cedar too, so you're familiar.
But this is really the point of the first noble truth, I think, and it's worth saying again.
The Buddha taught there was a first arrow and a second arrow.
The first arrow is the human experience.
It's the child dying.
The second arrow is the added layer of the story that we tell about our suffering.
It's the extra anguish.
It's the anguish that gets tied up with our sense of what we wanted or what should be or shouldn't be.
It's what we tell ourselves.
It's not about what really just happened.
It's our habitual, our conditioned reaction to it.
I think I told this group during this practice period one of my favorite stories about myself, so nod your heads if I start going in a direction you've recently heard.
It stands out because it was such a huge turning for me.
For many years I carried with me this really profound sense of loneliness that came from growing up in a certain kind of way.
I would come home at night from work and enter my back door going, nobody loves me, nobody cares.
No one was there but the dog.
And one day I walked in that back door and I saw myself do it again.
And I said, stop.
Just a story.
Life goes on.
It's actually pretty good.
But even if it weren't, that was just a habit.
It was like an *I Love Lucy* rerun playing in the background over and over again.
Our suffering is like that.
We believe ourselves in our lives to be something in particular, and so the difficulty that comes to us reverberates in that frame.
It's not to say that that frame doesn't have good causes, especially for childhood difficulties.
But the frame isn't useful, and it's not happening now.

That's what the Buddha was encouraging us to see, and what Thich Nhat Hanh was saying when he says, look at the things that you feed yourself, look at the voices that you listen to, look at your own stories that you tell yourself.
One view of really unpacking the first noble truth, and it's not an unusual Mahayana interpretation, is that to look for freedom from suffering is really to look at the three marks of existence.
We'll be studying those in the class this coming week, so this is a little appetizer.
The three marks are the identifiers of "this is Buddhism."
There are many different schools of Buddhism, many ways it's represented, many ways of entering into the practice.
The three main markers begin with impermanence.
That is, in time, the idea that things change with time.
What's really hard for us to get about that is that it means this person actually does change.

All these ideas that you have about yourself, or I have about myself, as being a certain kind of person: well, maybe I'm this tall, maybe I was born at a certain time, a certain place, but the actual workings and manifestations of this person moment by moment is changing.
It's changing right now as I watch your faces on the screen, how I'm coming, how you're responding to me and I'm responding in turn.
That actually has some effect on how I am in the world.
So together, there is this impermanence and changing.
I'm also pointing to there's no one separate here.
No self means that we don't operate independently, that this person right now speaking to you manifests completely out of unknown causes and conditions from time immemorial.

And with each of you and everyone else who has created the historical, cultural, sociological karma of this world, of this moment, of the generations of my adopted parents and my birth parents, all together right here in this room and this person.
There's no one separate from that.
All those influences are ongoing.
The other side of change and [unclear: "in substantiability"] is complete freedom.
It's complete freedom to respond and be in this moment, knowing that we are supported.
There's a line in one of the [unclear: "echoes"] that we chant, something like, *supported from all the cooperating factors seen and unseen throughout space and time.* It's like that.
They're nice words to hear.
I know them from my experience to have truth.
It takes a while to actually get that in your bones and understand it, but I believe that it's really there.
The Theravadan take on the first noble truth, and the way it's often talked about, is one of purification of the impediments of the mind.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** These are useful, and it's how we come to see how our mind operates, by looking at greed, hate and delusion.
But it's one dimension, and I think that's part of why it seems so burdensome to focus there.
Mahayana adds the side of the unknowable, or the insubstantiality or the boundlessness of our lives.
So the importance is not just lost, the idea of impermanence or no self, but it's actually gained.
It's gained to be so much more than our limiting ideas of ourselves usually think of ourselves.
And no substantial abiding self means an infinite interconnectedness with all beings.
Let me skip ahead a little bit, because I bet I'm starting to get close.
Desiree, am I getting close?
**Participant:** You're doing fine.
We have, I don't know, 15, 20 minutes?
Something like that.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** That includes talking time?
That'll give us about 20 minutes of discussion after.
Okay, great.
Thank you.
So just to say this again, this is a little redundant: in time, the fluidity of our life is like everything else.
It's like water moving.
Who we are as a person, it's easy to see in a big picture.
If you look back at things that were important to you when you were five, they're not so important now, right?
How you were, how you dressed, same thing in your 20s and on up.
You're moving.
It's a little harder to see the way the psychological shifts can work, because we have tendencies.
We have habits that we formed in terms of how we respond to situations and how we've learned to cope with situations.
But we're really not bound by those.
Many years ago, I was a sesshin director at Berkeley in a big, full zendo.
It was a five day sesshin.
It was very focused and concentrated.
And back in those days, the senior students, of which I was not yet one, carried the koi saku.
Do you know what that is?
That's the wake up stick that you sometimes see pictures of, of some ominous looking teacher walking behind people, behind their backs, carrying the stick and periodically going whack, whack to them.
Well, the koi saku is actually really wonderful.
We don't do it at Berkeley anymore, but we did in those days.
I was sesshin director, so I was facing out so I could see everything that was happening.
And one of the old students, who had been at that point a 30 plus year student, he's now a 50 plus year student, was carrying the koi saku and walking up my side of the [unclear: "ton"].
And it's very concentrated and very focused.
And Ron came up to someone to give the koi saku, who put their hands in gassho.
And this person somewhere off to the corner, I don't remember who it was, put his hands up and Ron went whack, whack.
And all of a sudden, it's like time stopped and the bottom dropped out.
And I understood that my father's complicated, twisted, complex, like all people, karma could stop.
Right there.
I didn't have the words for it until just last night as I was reading this.
Total stiffness.
He just was what he was.
And I just am what I am.
And all of a sudden, a part of my life started to move again.
A part of the storyline just shifted and dissolved like that.
I don't know how that happens exactly.
It doesn't really matter.
But the karma, the accumulated volitional actions, which are part of what gets reinforced by our thinking about things, just let itself cut itself free, like a dolphin that's been tied up in netting.
And the netting is cut and the dolphin can swim free again, just like that.
So that's impermanence.
And in a way, that's the insubstantiality of the self too.
Here's this idea set in stone that just dissolved.
And how did that happen?
Sixty people sitting quietly and concentratedly.
Many years of really sincere wanting to end the suffering that I was causing myself and others, but not directly.
We say in practice that it's like a soft rain or a lot of dew.
You don't realize that you're getting soaked through, but you are.
So I just want to say another word about the no self and no separate and abiding self that I think is really accessible and fun.
Do any of you listen to the podcast, My Unsung Hero?
It's a wonderful, wonderful podcast that's related to another podcast that a man named Shankar Vedant does about the social psychology of how mind works.
My Unsung Hero is a little five minute video posted once a week that asks people to call in with a story about someone who's changed their life.
And there are all kinds of stories.

The ones that I like are the strangers who stop in the middle of what they're doing, sometimes at a risk for themselves, like the two undocumented, presumably migrant workers who found this man who was stranded on a mountain road, having been bit by a scorpion.
He had rolled his car and was waiting for the paramedics or whomever, the police, to come rescue him.
These men stopped, had the traffic go around this car and waited with him until right when the police showed up, and then they just disappeared.
So stories like that, stories that have an impact on people so that they see the world a little differently and change it.
We're all co-created by each other in the moment, for the good or the bad, for what we bring to the situation.
Do you honk your horn at someone who cuts you off in traffic, or do you wish them a good day?
We're all constantly turning the Dharma wheel of karma.
There's no one who's separate from another person.
I have found that it's a relief to realize that in a fundamental way, it's impossible to live this life alone.
It's impossible to depend entirely upon yourself.
There's no such thing.
That's what Thich Nhat Hanh is always teaching when he says look into a flower.
You can see the compost, you can see the sun, you can see the hand of the gardener.
Nothing is separate from everything else.

And it's with those words that I can say now, after decades of practice, the experience that I had my first time walking into Soto Zen Zendo, when I bowed to my cushion and the two people bowed on either side and I burst into tears, tears of relief.
I wasn't alone.
Tears of relief.
I don't do it by myself.
We're all walking this path together.
And a relief that there's goodness in everyone, even when you can't see it, even when it's not so evident at all.
There's a yearning for happiness, if not wholeness.
And to quote the Lotus Sutra, everyone will be a Buddha someday.
Everyone who turns their way itself in that direction will be a Buddha someday.
That is a great healing from our separation.
The third mark of existence is dukkha, right?
That's how it's usually translated, the unsatisfactoriness of a life.

But in the Mahayana, there's a way of seeing through the ideas of who we are and what our circumstances are, to be unbound by our limited thinking, to realize that we are multitudes, the multitudes of which Walt Whitman spoke.
To die the death of no death, meaning to not be the person that you thought you were, isn't there.
The person that you are contains everything, contains every possibility.
I don't mean that quite literally, but perhaps you understand it to mean to be much more expansive, inclusive, to have possibilities.
This is the healing and transformation of Buddhism.
There was this debate that happened on this listserv.

Some groups, or some teachers, have come to see for themselves that they feel like they need to teach one stream as a kind of healing, psychological transformation, and another for the people who are more serious or have a spiritual call.
But actually, there's no way to take those two apart.
There's just where your inclination or orientation is for how you want to live your life, I think.
So the three marks, this is another build out of this talk.
And if I have maybe five or ten more minutes, I want to say something even more provocative.
**Participant:** About five minutes.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Five minutes, I can do that.
So the three marks of existence: for me, the most important or the real driver of the eightfold double path is right view.
And I see right view as directly related to seeing impermanence for what it is in this transformative way, seeing no self also in this way that is boundlessness.
It's another way of saying that emptiness is not devoid of everything, but it's inclusive of everything.
And that opens life up in a really profound way.
So in seeing this interpending existence, there really is nothing lacking.
This last week, I got a wedding announcement from someone who had been an AmeriCorps volunteer at my workplace 15 years ago.
We had lightly been in touch, a really wonderful young man who had been lost in his spiritual seeking.
He came to Berkeley Zen Center for a while.
And I knew he had gone on to divinity school, but I didn't know exactly what he had done.
He had always been uncertain in himself.
And in this picture, it was his wedding pictures, he was so comfortable in his body, not just happy as a bride or a groom would be.
So comfortable and at ease.
It gave me such great joy.
And I thought, some people seeing that, and me at another time, might have also had a pang of what I didn't have.
But I felt filled up by seeing this old student I hadn't talked to in 15 years.
The greed appetite is satisfied because nothing is not mine.
There's plenty to go around.
And so the unhooking of some of the difficulties of the Second Noble Truth can be seen through the lens of no self and impermanence.
And for impermanence, for me, that understanding is that nothing is ever out of place.
Things change as a result of everything that's gone before it.
And all of our volitional actions over centuries and time, including mine and my choices in this moment.

This is the idea of the analogy of being shot by an arrow that the Buddha used, and how some of us will look around for the culprit, will analyze the arrow, will ask what if we had been going down another path, we wouldn't have been hit, and all of that.
Who knows the roots and the causes, the conditions of what happens to us?
It's completely unknowable.
That's part of what karma really is.
Buddha said it's one of the unknowables that will drive you crazy if you try and figure it out.
Literally, that's in the Pali Canon.
Circumstances have no thought of us or our lives.
We might be innocent bystanders, or bring a lot of our own volitional behavior to contribute to how this moment arises.
But from karma's standpoint, from the workings of the world, there's no moral [unclear: "valency"].
There's no good or bad.
It's just a neutral and objective way.
That doesn't mean that we don't want to act in a way according to our values, according to the precepts.
But there's no absolute in what's happening.
There's no good or bad.
There's just our response.
So in reality, there is no source of suffering.
There is no definitive source of suffering.
It's all created.
It's all fluid.
It's all impermanent.
That's a really hard thing to swallow, I think, when you really look at it.
All we have to do is look at the news.
All we have to do is see what's happening on the Syrian border with Turkey or in the Ukraine or with any of the videos of police brutality that are viewed before us.
And we can't believe there's no source of suffering and that it shouldn't be that way.
But the moral valence of the universe is really neutral.
It's our actions that make a difference.
And if we look deeply, we understand how unknowable it is, and actually how we can empathize.
How could five African American policemen, do they need a job?
Do they want to be someone in their community?
Do they want to be able to protect themselves or prove that they belong to the club of cops to get along?
They have their own internalized sense of racism and wanting to differentiate oneself.
Did they grow up in a culture that says they couldn't do differently?
It goes on deeper and deeper and deeper.
And all you can do is really have great empathy for how unknowable and how human it is.
I think this is how I'll say for myself, it's a great relief to know that, quote, nothing went wrong.
That doesn't mean that there isn't something to do about it.
It doesn't mean that things are all right the way they are.
But in a Buddhist frame, they're understandable.
So by clear seeing, the hopelessness is transformed into a way forward.

The way forward is the way that you act out of the wisdom of understanding the complexity of what's to be addressed in this moment, and your own compassion, by joining human heart to human heart, human sentiment and desire for happiness and ease.
So Buddha's right view is neutral and takes everything in its place.
It cannot remove the sorrow of a human life or the joys of a human body and heart.
And it frees us to live our life unburdened by the limitations of our usual karmic mind.
To answer the question for ourselves, for each of us, for our own selves, out of these five personal skandhas called Desiree or Bob, John or Michael or Reina.
That's the big question.
How do you respond?
So thank you very much.
That's my offering for you.
Thank you for your rapt attention.
I really look forward to your responses and your own workings of what I'm talking about.
